result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.number_of_spanning_trees()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Count the spanning trees of the graph (Kirchhoff's matrix-tree theorem). ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L47039-L47155){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.number_of_spanning_trees( root=None, weighted=None, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Number of spanning trees](/assets/graphs/number-of-spanning-trees.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Left: a square A, B, C, D with the diagonal A–C in the accent color. Right: its 8 spanning trees as miniatures in two rows. The top row holds the 4 trees of the plain square, each dropping one side; the bottom row holds the 4 trees that use the diagonal. The heading gives the count, 8, and a note under the rows the sum 4 + 4 = 8." width="100%"} A spanning tree connects all `n` nodes with `n - 1` edges and no cycle. Counting them measures redundancy: a tree has exactly one spanning tree (lose any edge and it falls apart), while a complete graph on `n` nodes has $n^{n-2}$ (Cayley's formula). The count is used as a reliability measure for communication networks, in statistical physics and in enumerative combinatorics, and it can be huge even for small graphs. On a directed graph, the method counts spanning arborescences rooted at `root=`: trees in which every node can be reached from the root along edge directions. On a weighted graph (or with `weighted=True`), each tree counts as the product of its edge weights, which gives the normalizing constant for sampling trees in proportion to their weight (see `random_spanning_tree()`); pass `weighted=False` for a plain count. Parallel edges count as distinct (each choice gives a different tree) and self-loops are ignored. A disconnected graph has no spanning tree, so the result is `0`. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [root]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str, None]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Required on a directed graph, where it is the root of the arborescences (as an integer ID or string label). Ignored on undirected graphs. [weighted]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Whether to weight each tree by the product of its edge weights. If `None` (default), follows the graph's `weighted` flag. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [int or float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Unweighted counts are exact integers, however large. Weighted counts are floats. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph is empty, or `root=` is missing or unknown on a directed graph. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} By Kirchhoff's theorem the number of spanning trees equals any cofactor of the Laplacian $L = D - A$: delete one row and the matching column and take the determinant. For arborescences rooted at $r$ (Tutte's directed version) the in-degree Laplacian is used and the row and column of $r$ are deleted. Unweighted determinants are computed exactly: with Bareiss' fraction-free elimination in 128-bit integers when the intermediate values fit, and otherwise modulo enough 61-bit primes to exceed Hadamard's bound on the determinant, combined with the Chinese remainder theorem. Each pass costs $O(V^3)$ operations. Weighted determinants use a floating-point LU decomposition. ## Examples {.doc-examples} A 4-cycle has four spanning trees (drop any one edge), and adding a diagonal raises the count to eight: ::: {#a8489301 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec square = ec.Graph().add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D"]) square.add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "D"), ("D", "A")]) before = square.number_of_spanning_trees() square.add_edge("A", "C") # Returns (4, 8) before, square.number_of_spanning_trees() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (4, 8) ``` ::: ::: Cayley's formula gives $6^4 = 1296$ for the complete graph on six nodes: ::: {#b5454dde .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} ec.Graph().add_full_graph(6).number_of_spanning_trees() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 1296 ``` ::: ::: On a directed graph the count depends on the root. This directed triangle with an extra edge A -> C has two arborescences rooted at A (A -> B -> C, and A -> B with A -> C) but only one rooted at B (B -> C -> A): ::: {#3f50435c .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} d = ec.Graph(directed=True).add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) d.add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "A"), ("A", "C")]) d.number_of_spanning_trees(root="A"), d.number_of_spanning_trees(root="B") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` (2, 1) ``` ::: :::
